question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old woman was assessed this morning in the ambulatory procedure suite prior to excision of a slowly enlarging 8-mm pigmented nevus just superior to the right scapular tip; dermatologic surgery anticipates local anesthetic infiltration, a 2-cm fusiform ellipse, and layered closure completed within thirty minutes, with discharge expected two hours after the last vital-sign check. She walked briskly from the parking garage, climbed two flights of stairs without pause, and set her handbag on the stretcher before changing into the gown, stating that she jogs three miles four times a week and teaches a weekend yoga class, thus maintaining full baseline activity. The patient has not entered an operating theatre, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology bay in recent months, there have been no hospitalizations, emergency visits, or urgent care encounters for any reason during that interval, and she has not undergone any major surgical procedure in the past month. She denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-extremity edema that indents with pressure, exertional chest discomfort, exercise intolerance, or episodes of sudden weight gain; the most recent transthoracic echocardiogram, obtained five years ago during a murmur evaluation, showed normal chamber sizes and preserved left-ventricular ejection fraction. Past injuries are limited to a childhood wrist sprain; she has never required a splint, cast, traction device, or wheelchair, and has avoided falls, vehicular collisions, long-bone fractures, concussive head trauma, or spinal cord insult, and she has not worn any immobilizing plaster cast or experienced any hip, pelvis, or leg fracture within the past month. Respiratory history is unremarkable—she has never smoked, lives in a pet-free home, has no chronic cough, wheeze, seasonal bronchial trouble, or diagnosis of chronic bronchitis or emphysema. The review of systems is likewise negative for recent fever, chills, purulent sputum, urinary tract irritation, abdominal pain, or constitutional symptoms. She does, however, report a network of bluish, serpiginous superficial veins along the posteromedial calves that first appeared during her second pregnancy and have gradually become more prominent when she stands for prolonged periods in her occupation as a high-school chemistry teacher; these veins ache at the end of a long lecture day but do not cause swelling, skin discoloration, or ulceration, and she wears 15–20 mm Hg knee-high compression stockings on school days for comfort. She has never experienced unilateral calf tenderness, sudden leg girth change, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, or unexplained dyspnea, and duplex imaging has never been ordered. Of note, her mother developed a clot in the calf veins one week after a Cesarean section and required several months of warfarin, and an older brother was admitted in his early forties with a saddle embolus following a trans-Pacific flight; prompted by that pedigree, the patient underwent outpatient hematology evaluation three years ago, during which polymerase-chain-reaction testing revealed heterozygosity for the G20210A mutation in the prothrombin gene. She was counseled on long-haul flight precautions and advised to avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives but was not started on chronic anticoagulation. Her current medication list is limited to a daily multivitamin and intermittent ibuprofen for tension headaches; she takes no hormones, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or selective estrogen receptor modulators. Alcohol intake is an occasional glass of red wine with dinner on weekends, and she does not use nicotine or illicit substances. On physical examination today she is seated comfortably, alert, and oriented, with a body mass index of 23 kg/m². Temperature is 36.6 °C, heart rate 72 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 14 /min, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and cardiac auscultation reveals a soft grade II/VI midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border without gallop. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender with normal bowel sounds and no hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower limbs shows clusters of dilated tortuous superficial veins along the long saphenous territory bilaterally, more pronounced when she dangles the legs; there is no pitting, the skin is warm and intact, calf diameters are equal, and gentle dorsiflexion elicits no discomfort. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves II–XII, full motor strength, and symmetric reflexes. The back lesion planned for excision is well circumscribed with even pigment and no ulceration or surrounding erythema. A single 22-gauge peripheral catheter inserted into the left forearm delivers lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; no ports, tunneled catheters, or peripherally inserted central lines are present. Morning laboratories obtained by fingerstick and venipuncture reveal hemoglobin 13.7 g/dL, platelet count 242 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, AST 21 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, prothrombin time 11.8 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 bpm with no ST-T abnormalities, and a screening chest radiograph performed for pre-operative clearance depicts clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette. She has been fasting since midnight, used her usual compression hosiery during the drive in, and expresses understanding of leg-pump application before transport to the minor procedure room.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score sums weighted perioperative venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk factors.
- Age 47 (41–60 years): 1 point.
- Planned minor surgery (skin excision lasting about 30 minutes, under 45 minutes): 1 point.
- Visible varicose veins in both calves: 1 point, counted once.
- Family history of VTE (mother with DVT and brother with PE): 3 points, counted once regardless of the number of affected relatives.
- Known inherited thrombophilia (heterozygous prothrombin G20210A mutation): 3 points, separate from family history.
No additional factors are documented: she is mobile, has BMI 23, uses no estrogen, and has no personal VTE history or central venous catheter. Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 3 = 9.
Final answer: 9
